body.objective: Students will be able to play at different dynamic levels.

successCriteria: I can name and play dynamic levels from piano to forte

body.hook: Imagine a movie where every actor shouts every line. Music without dynamics is the same: flat and tiring. Changing volume is how bands create drama, calm and excitement.

vocabulary.definition: The loudness or softness of music.

study.title: Loud and Soft
study.question: How do dynamics make music expressive?
study.passage:
Dynamics ladder (written for this lesson): pp (pianissimo, very soft), p (piano), mp (mezzo piano), mf (mezzo forte), f (forte), ff (fortissimo, very loud).
Rules of tone: Soft is not weak: keep air support; use less air, not less energy. Loud is not harsh: more air, but keep the tone round and don't force it.
Activities: 1. Ladder: play Concert B♭ for 4 counts at each level, p, mp, mf, f. Partner checks: does the pitch stay steady? 2. Crescendo: 8 counts from p to f; decrescendo 8 counts f to p. Spread the change evenly ("no sudden jumps"). 3. Hairpin game: the conductor's left hand rises (louder) or lowers (softer); play to match. 4. Band: play a 4-bar line twice, first all at mf, then with written dynamics (p, cresc., f, decresc.). Which is more interesting?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Play one note at four levels

body.hook: A concert piece doesn't come together in one rehearsal. Bands break pieces into small sections, fix tricky spots and slowly build up to performance tempo, the way athletes train for a game.

study.title: Building a Concert Piece
study.question: How do musicians prepare a piece for performance?
study.passage:
Rehearsal plan (written for this lesson):
1. Road map (5 minutes): Look through the concert piece: tempo, key signature, repeats, rehearsal letters (A, B, C) and dynamics.
2. Find tricky spots (5 minutes): circle up to three bars that are hardest for you.
3. Fix them (15 minutes): clap and count the rhythm; play at a slow tempo (e.g. 60 BPM) with a metronome; repeat correctly three times in a row; increase by 4–8 BPM; then add the bar before and after ("chunking").
4. Full band (15 minutes): rehearse from rehearsal letters, listening for balance and togetherness.
5. Practice log and goal (5 minutes): write today's tempo for each tricky spot and a goal for next rehearsal (e.g. "Bar 17 at 88 BPM"). Home practice: 15–20 minutes, starting with long tones, then tricky spots, then the whole piece.

successCriteria: I can follow concert etiquette as a performer

body.hook: A concert starts before the first note. How you walk on, sit, wait and bow tells the audience you're a professional. Concert etiquette is the polish on all your hard work.

study.title: Showtime
study.question: How do musicians act professionally on stage?
study.passage:
Concert checklist (written for this lesson):
Before: concert dress as your teacher sets (often black and white); instrument clean, reeds checked, valve oil and spare reeds packed; music in order in a folder; arrive at call time.
On stage: walk on quietly in order, sit, place music; rest position (instrument on lap or held still) between pieces; no talking, waving or looking at the audience.
Ready: when the conductor raises their arms, move to ready position together.
After each piece: hold still until the conductor lowers their arms; then stand when signalled for applause.
Audience etiquette: silence phones; clap at the end of a piece, not between movements; stay seated during pieces; enter or leave only between pieces.
After the concert: self-assessment: rate tone, rhythm, dynamics, togetherness and stage behaviour 1–4 with one sentence each, and set one goal for the next concert.
Practise: a full dress rehearsal of walking on, ready position, playing and bowing.
